answers.answer: The company name is not in the question, so a query built from the question alone cannot search for the headquarters fact; what has to be retrieved second depends on what the first retrieval produced. One retrieval from the input is sufficient when the information needs are clear in the user's input and retrieving relevant knowledge once from that input alone is enough.
accept: the second fact cannot be queried because the entity it depends on is not in the original question
what to retrieve next depends on what has already been retrieved or derived
names the stated condition: information needs clear in the input and one retrieval from the input alone sufficient

answers.answer: IRCoT alternates extending the chain of thought, using the question plus the paragraphs collected so far plus the reasoning sentences so far to produce the next sentence, with expanding the retrieved set, using that last reasoning sentence as the retrieval query. It repeats until the chain of thought reports an answer or the maximum number of reasoning steps is reached.
accept: one step generates the next chain-of-thought sentence from the question, collected paragraphs and prior sentences
the other step retrieves more paragraphs using the last reasoning sentence as the query
stops when the chain of thought states an answer or a maximum step count is hit

answers.answer: In IRCoT the timing belongs to the system: a retrieval happens after every reasoning sentence, regardless of whether the model needed one, even though the query text comes from the model. In FLARE the timing belongs to the generator: it predicts the upcoming sentence and only retrieves when that prediction contains low-confidence tokens, then regenerates the sentence. The trigger sits in a different component, so a system that never faces uncertainty retrieves on every step under IRCoT and not at all under FLARE.
accept: IRCoT retrieves on a fixed schedule of one retrieval per reasoning step, set by the system
FLARE retrieves when its own predicted next sentence contains low-confidence tokens
identifies that the difference is which component holds the trigger, not how often retrieval happens to fire

answers.answer: You build a classifier, a smaller language model that consumes the incoming query and predicts its complexity, trained on labels collected automatically from the actual predicted outcomes of models and from inductive biases in the datasets. It runs per query, before generation begins, and selects between no retrieval, single-step retrieval, and iterative multi-step retrieval.
accept: a separate smaller model or classifier that predicts query complexity
it runs per query before generation starts, not during generation
it selects among no retrieval, single-step retrieval and iterative retrieval

answers.answer: It holds lightweight identifiers such as file paths, stored queries, and web links, rather than the data itself, and loads the content into context at runtime through tools when it is needed. The article states this as a recommendation and as an observation of what teams are doing; it publishes no measurement behind either.
accept: identifiers such as file paths, stored queries or links are held instead of the content
content is loaded into context at runtime through tools at the point of need
the cited article offers no measurement, only a recommendation and an observation

answers.answer: It increases the overheads and the cost of generation, because the model has to be activated once per retrieval, and without caching the previous activations are recomputed after each retrieval. The paper states this as an assertion about what a naive implementation does, with no cost figure attached, rather than as a measurement.
accept: the model is activated once per retrieval
a caching-free implementation recomputes previous activations after each retrieval
it is an assertion about implementation, not a measured cost

answers.answer: IRCoT's recall gain is measured against one-step retrieve-and-read with a BM25 lexical retriever, so it is a retrieval metric against a retrieve-once baseline. Self-Ask's gain is measured against self-ask without the search engine, where the model answers its own follow-up questions from its parameters, which is closer to a no-retrieval baseline, and it is an answer metric. Different baselines, different metrics, and different models, so ranking one against the other compares nothing.
accept: IRCoT's baseline is one-step or single-time retrieval and the number is a retrieval recall figure
Self-Ask's baseline is self-ask answering sub-questions from parametric knowledge, closer to no retrieval, and the number is an answer accuracy figure
concludes that numbers measured against different baselines or metrics cannot be ranked

answers.answer: On ELI5, neither single-time retrieval nor FLARE gave significant gains over not retrieving at all. On Wizard of Wikipedia, the authors point to the short output, about 20 tokens on average, as the reason multiple disparate retrievals were not called for, and they hedge that explanation rather than measuring it. Together they say that on-demand retrieval pays only when the output is long enough to need information the question did not already cover.
accept: ELI5: neither single-time retrieval nor FLARE beat not retrieving
Wizard of Wikipedia: output around 20 tokens on average, given as the reason multiple retrievals were not needed
draws the conclusion that the mechanism needs a long or multi-fact output to have anything to work with
